committeeQuestion.question: Which control in your highest-impact AI workflow would you test first, and what result would force a change?
committeeQuestion.why: The Bank of England/FCA survey found policies more widely reported than ongoing monitoring, leakage testing or periodic review. It records firm responses; it does not test whether those controls work.
committeeQuestion.evidence: One recent monitoring event, its linked decision, the associated leakage-test or recertification result, and a dated change made when a threshold was breached.

committeeQuestions.question: How do you validate and reverse a high-materiality vendor model update before it reaches a critical workflow?
committeeQuestions.why: The survey found reported practices varied; regression testing and rollback were not universal. Some reported bases are small and should be read cautiously.
committeeQuestions.evidence: A recent vendor update with test results, an approval boundary, the rollback trigger and evidence the rollback path works.

committeeQuestions.question: If a Python environment ran LiteLLM 1.107.0, can you identify the credentials it could reach without starting Python in that environment?
committeeQuestions.why: Microsoft reports the compromised package could execute via Python startup files even where an application did not import LiteLLM.
committeeQuestions.evidence: Affected environment inventory, preserved forensic evidence, reachable-secret scope, credential rotation and a clean rebuild or recovery record.

judgement.title: Policy adoption is not control evidence.
judgement.editorialAngle: Use the new Bank of England/FCA survey to test the gap between reported AI policy adoption and post-deployment control evidence, while treating the survey as descriptive rather than a control test.
judgement.distinctFromPrevious: Edition 19 asked who defines and enforces an agent’s authority outside the agent. Edition 20 shifts to whether controls remain observable and effective across material AI use after deployment, vendor change and software compromise.
judgement.observation: The Bank of England and FCA’s 2026 survey found firm-wide AI policies at 94% of full-survey respondents; ongoing monitoring, leakage testing and periodic review or recertification were each reported by about half. Eighty per cent reported AI agents deployed and 2% broad autonomy. Response bases vary by question.
judgement.executiveJudgement: Approval is a snapshot; controls must follow the live workflow. A model or vendor change can invalidate its approval assumptions. The survey reports coverage, not effectiveness, so it cannot show whether monitoring catches the shift.
judgement.implication: Choose one high-impact workflow changed since its last review. Have its owner replay the relevant alert—or trigger a controlled threshold breach—measure detection-to-decision time, and record whether use was revised, restricted or retained, with a dated reason.
judgement.archiveCorrection: Editorial update (2 Nov 2026): ‘Why it matters’ and ‘What to do’ were revised to clarify the inference and specify a measurable post-approval control test. The reported survey figures and publication date are unchanged.

weeklyReadout.heading: Which AI control still works after go-live?
steps: Select a high-impact AI workflow with a model, data or vendor change since its last review.
Replay the relevant monitoring alert or trigger a controlled threshold breach.
Measure detection-to-decision time and record whether use was revised, restricted or retained, with a reason.
Assign the first unproven step to an owner with a due date.

topSignals.title: AI policies are more common than post-deployment controls
topSignals.label: Bank of England/FCA supervisory survey
topSignals.why: The 2026 survey reports AI governance arrangements across 196 firms. Among full-survey respondents, 94% reported firm-wide policies, while key post-deployment data controls were each reported by about half. This is descriptive evidence, not a control-effectiveness test.
topSignals.source: Primary / Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority / 2026-10-26

topSignals.title: LiteLLM compromise turns package startup into credential risk
topSignals.label: Software supply-chain incident analysis
topSignals.why: Microsoft says malicious startup files in LiteLLM 1.107.0 could run when Python started, even without an application importing the gateway. Exposure may extend to development, CI/CD, test and container environments.

topSignals.title: OpenAI reports stronger containment after frontier-model boundary tests
topSignals.label: Provider security disclosure
topSignals.why: OpenAI describes hardened containment for its own research environments and a high-compute red-team campaign. The account is company-reported; it does not independently establish resilience in customer deployments.

topSignals.title: Anthropic’s S-1 puts compute commitments and provider economics in view
topSignals.label: SEC-filed S-1
topSignals.why: Anthropic’s preliminary filing exposes compute commitments and provider economics, while leaving key offering terms blank. It is useful evidence about provider dependencies, not a priced or completed IPO.
topSignals.source: Primary / Anthropic, PBC / U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission / 2026-10-26

topSignals.title: Historical KeyDrift activity exposes Cisco SD-WAN control-plane compromise paths
topSignals.label: Threat analysis · historical activity
topSignals.why: Cisco Talos reports historical exploitation of an authentication-bypass flaw in SD-WAN controllers and malware designed to collect keying material. Preserve the source’s historical scope; check exposure and patch status.
